business.overview:
CoreWeave rents GPU-accelerated compute and related storage, networking and managed software under capacity contracts. Revenue is driven by deployed clusters, contracted utilization, pricing and the speed with which powered shells become billable infrastructure.

The direct AI transmission channel is customer demand for training and inference on NVIDIA systems: signed commitments support datacenter and GPU purchases, and completed deployments convert backlog into cloud revenue. Active power of 1.5 GW versus roughly 3.7 GW contracted shows both the opportunity and the delivery gap.

The model breaks if a concentrated customer base delays workloads, facilities or chips arrive late, power is unavailable, or debt and lease funding becomes uneconomic. Because capex and interest precede revenue, even a modest commissioning delay can damage liquidity and equity value before it appears in backlog. Commissioning discipline must therefore be judged quarter by quarter against active power, capital expenditure, interest expense and customer collections, rather than inferred from the nominal backlog alone.
business.moat: The advantage is deployment scale: scarce GPU allocations, power contracts, datacenter sites and orchestration software assembled into large clusters that few new entrants can finance quickly. It is not a low-capital software moat; counterparties, lenders and NVIDIA remain essential inputs.

business.overview:
Applied Digital develops and operates high-density campuses, earning recurring base rent, tenant fit-out revenue and expense recoveries from HPC customers; it also retains a smaller datacenter-hosting operation. The AI transmission channel is direct but physical: hyperscalers and model developers contract critical IT capacity, Applied Digital finances and builds the powered shell, and rent begins as halls are delivered. The $36 billion initial contracted-revenue figure is therefore a long-duration construction and occupancy schedule, not current-period sales.

The model breaks through project delays, cost overruns, unavailable power, tenant concentration or financing terms that shift too much value to creditors and preferred holders. Fit-out revenue can also flatter growth while base rent is still ramping, so segment NOI and delivered MW matter more than consolidated revenue alone. business.moat: APLD's defensible asset is a portfolio of power-secured, high-density campuses with signed anchor tenants and demonstrated early delivery at Polaris Forge 1. The moat remains project-specific: it can erode through construction slippage, contract renegotiation or a higher cost of capital.

The AI transmission channel is direct: model builders and enterprises reserve accelerators, often prepaying to secure capacity; Nebius uses those commitments to finance GPUs and datacenters, then recognizes cloud revenue as service is delivered. The model breaks if GPU pricing compresses, customer prepayments reverse into delivery disputes, power or equipment arrives late, or capital raised through converts and equity fails to produce adequate returns. The decisive evidence will be recognized revenue, deployed megawatts and cash payback after financing costs, not contract count or prepayment inflows viewed independently.
business.moat: Nebius combines GPU access, purpose-built datacenters, cloud software and unusually large customer prepayments. Its reported one-year-ten-month payback and Q2 ACV above $20M per MW suggest attractive current unit economics, but those economics are vulnerable to competition and falling compute prices.

business.overview:
Core Scientific develops high-density datacenters and sells colocation capacity under long-term contracts, while retaining a smaller digital-asset mining operation. Revenue is driven by billable megawatts, contractual pricing, power pass-throughs, uptime and residual mining hash economics.

The AI transmission channel is direct: customers such as CoreWeave and AMD reserve power and datacenter infrastructure, Core Scientific funds the conversion and build, and contracted fees begin as capacity is delivered. Billing power of 437 MW in mid-July versus 1.1 GW leased quantifies the remaining conversion runway.

The model breaks if construction is late, customer credit weakens, equipment or grid delivery fails, or financing covenants constrain the build. Potential contract value above $24B is undiscounted and delivered over many years. Warrant accounting can obscure operating results, while actual capex and liquidity determine whether common shareholders capture the residual economics. Investors should therefore track billing megawatts, customer acceptance, incremental rent and remaining construction cost together, rather than valuing the entire leased pipeline at an undiscounted contract headline.
business.moat: Core Scientific controls large powered campuses and has already demonstrated conversion from mining to billable HPC colocation. Its edge is speed-to-power and signed counterparties, but it remains capital-dependent and cannot rely on contract value alone to defend returns.

business.overview:
Bloom manufactures and installs solid-oxide fuel-cell systems that generate electricity on site, and it earns product, installation and service-related revenue. Sales depend on system shipments, project acceptance, pricing, manufacturing yield and the long-term performance of the installed fleet.

The AI transmission channel is behind-the-meter power: datacenter operators can deploy Bloom servers where grid interconnection is delayed, converting natural gas or biogas into electricity without waiting for full transmission upgrades. Higher product revenue therefore reflects actual equipment delivery rather than remote exposure to AI spending.
